question: How did the righteous LORD intervene to liberate His afflicted people in Psalm 129:4?
opt1: The LORD is mighty: He hath broken the iron chariots of Pharaoh
opt2: The LORD is holy: He hath rained fire upon the towers of Babylon
opt3: The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked
opt4: The LORD is our shield: He hath scattered the heathen with a whirlwind
correct: The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked
explanation: God severed the harness cords of the wicked plowmen, breaking the yoke-ropes that bound Israel to their oppressive furrowing. Psalm 129:4 (KJV) - "The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked."

question: What judgment is invoked against all who hate Zion in Psalm 129:5?
opt1: Let them be delivered to the sword and their cities burned with fire
opt2: Let them be carried away captive into the trackless wilderness
opt3: Let their names be blotted out from under the heavens of the LORD
opt4: Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion
correct: Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion
explanation: All adversaries who oppose God's kingdom and holy city are condemned to shameful confusion and humiliating military retreat. Psalm 129:5 (KJV) - "Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion."

question: To what fragile, short-lived vegetation are the enemies of Zion compared in Psalm 129:6?
opt1: The grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up
opt2: The wild weeds in the desert that dry up at noon
opt3: The chaff of the summer threshingfloor driven by wind
opt4: The mushrooms of the night that melt in the morning sun
correct: The grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up
explanation: Seeds germinating on shallow, dirt-plastered flat roofs sprout rapidly after rain, but lack root depth, withering completely before even maturing. Psalm 129:6 (KJV) - "Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up:"

question: What total lack of harvest value characterizes this rooftop grass in Psalm 129:7?
opt1: Wherewith no bread can be baked for the hunger of the poor
opt2: Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom
opt3: Which the cattle refuse to eat and the sheep trample into dust
opt4: Which the fire of the oven consumeth without giving any heat
correct: Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom
explanation: The wicked produce zero lasting harvest: no reaper can gather a handful, nor can any sheaf-binder carry an armful to the threshing floor. Psalm 129:7 (KJV) - "Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom."

question: What traditional harvest greeting (such as Boaz gave in Ruth 2:4) is denied to the wicked in Psalm 129:8?
opt1: Peace be unto your house, and health unto your cattle
opt2: May the God of Abraham multiply your grain and your wine
opt3: The blessing of the LORD be upon you: we bless you in the name of the LORD
opt4: Joy to your threshingfloor, and prosperity to your storehouses
correct: The blessing of the LORD be upon you: we bless you in the name of the LORD
explanation: Passersby traditionally hailed reapers with cheerful benedictions ('The blessing of the LORD be upon you'); but for Zion's haters, no blessing can be spoken. Psalm 129:8 (KJV) - "Neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the LORD be upon you: we bless you in the name of the LORD."

question: To what historical era in Israel's corporate memory does 'from my youth' refer in verses 1 and 2?
opt1: The reign of King Saul before David was anointed
opt2: The time of the Maccabean revolt against the Greeks
opt3: The building of the second temple under Zerubbabel
opt4: The Egyptian servitude and the Exodus era, when Israel was formed as a young nation (Hosea 11:1)
correct: The Egyptian servitude and the Exodus era, when Israel was formed as a young nation (Hosea 11:1)
explanation: Prophets consistently identify Egypt as Israel's national 'youth': 'When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt' (Hosea 11:1). Psalm 129:1-2 (KJV) - "Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say: Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth: yet they have not prevailed against me."

question: What theological attribute of God is highlighted in verse 4 as the reason for Israel's liberation from the wicked plowmen?
opt1: His righteousness ('The LORD is righteous')
opt2: His omnipotence
opt3: His mercy
opt4: His jealousy
correct: His righteousness ('The LORD is righteous')
explanation: Because God is righteous, He cannot permit unjust cruelty and persecution to perpetuate unchecked; His judicial rectitude severs the cords of oppression. Psalm 129:4 (KJV) - "The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked."

question: What is the primary spiritual lesson of Psalm 129 for the historic people of God?
opt1: That agriculture on stone housetops is forbidden under Mosaic ceremonial law
opt2: The invincibility of God's covenant church: though brutally persecuted across centuries, she is indestructible because the Lord cuts the cords of her oppressors
opt3: That reapers should never greet travelers along the highways of Judea
opt4: That Israel had never suffered any defeats in battle throughout her history
correct: The invincibility of God's covenant church: though brutally persecuted across centuries, she is indestructible because the Lord cuts the cords of her oppressors
explanation: The psalm is an anthem of divine preservation: persecutors strike deep blows, yet can never ultimately prevail against God's indestructible covenant community. Psalm 129:2, 4 (KJV) - "Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth: yet they have not prevailed against me ... The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked."

question: From what desperate spiritual location does the penitent author cry out to God in Psalm 130:1?
opt1: From the highest pinnacles of Zion have I lifted my prayer
opt2: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD
opt3: In the assembly of the elders have I poured out my heart
opt4: From the dust of the wilderness have I called upon thy name
correct: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD
explanation: The soul cries from the overwhelming subterranean abyss of guilt, helplessness, and acute conviction of personal sin. Psalm 130:1 (KJV) - "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD."

question: What searching theological rhetorical question does the psalmist pose concerning divine scrutiny of sin in Psalm 130:3?
opt1: If God should measure our sins by the law, where is our salvation?
opt2: Can a mortal man be pure before his Maker, or righteous before God?
opt3: If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?
opt4: Shall the dust give thanks unto the Lord, or declare His truth in Sheol?
correct: If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?
explanation: If God kept a strict, unforgiving ledger of human sins ('mark iniquities'), not a single human being on earth could withstand His judicial audit. Psalm 130:3 (KJV) - "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?"

question: What glorious redemptive truth is declared in Psalm 130:4, and what is its ultimate holy purpose?
opt1: For there is mercy with the King, that the wicked may repent
opt2: For thou delightest in sacrifice, that thy house may be honored
opt3: For thy covenant is everlasting, that Israel may conquer all nations
opt4: But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared
correct: But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared
explanation: Forgiveness is God's prerogative; its fruit is not cheap presumption or license, but profound holy awe, reverent devotion, and loving obedience. Psalm 130:4 (KJV) - "But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared."

question: Upon what foundation does the waiting believer anchor his hope in Psalm 130:5?
opt1: I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope
opt2: I wait for the vision of the night, and in the signs of heaven do I hope
opt3: I wait for the smoke of the morning incense, and in the altar do I hope
opt4: I wait for the decree of the king, and in the strength of Zion do I hope
correct: I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope
explanation: Faith is not rooted in subjective emotional feelings, but in patient, resolute trust anchored in the unshakeable promises of God's written Word. Psalm 130:5 (KJV) - "I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope."

question: What vivid watchman simile expresses the intensity of the psalmist's longing for God in Psalm 130:6?
opt1: My soul thirsteth for God as a parched traveler in the desert sands
opt2: My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning
opt3: My heart panteth for the sanctuary as the hart panteth after the water brooks
opt4: Mine eyes wait for salvation as a sentry waiting for the king's chariot
correct: My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning
explanation: Like weary, cold city sentinels stationed on dark city walls eagerly watching for the first glimmer of dawn, the soul yearns for the light of God's presence. Psalm 130:6 (KJV) - "My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning."

question: What two divine attributes encourage all Israel to place their hope in the LORD in Psalm 130:7?
opt1: For with the LORD there is eternal strength, and with Him is royal majesty
opt2: For with the LORD there is righteous judgment, and with Him is infinite power
opt3: For with the LORD there is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption
opt4: For with the LORD there is holy wrath, and with Him is vengeance on foes
correct: For with the LORD there is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption
explanation: God's redemptive resources are inexhaustible: abundant covenant steadfast love (chesed) and overflowing, all-sufficient redemption (pedut). Psalm 130:7 (KJV) - "Let Israel hope in the LORD: for with the LORD there is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption."

question: What comprehensive promise of total national salvation concludes Psalm 130 in verse 8?
opt1: And He shall deliver Zion from the hands of the Philistines
opt2: And He shall establish the throne of David throughout all generations
opt3: And He shall bring back the exiles from the four corners of the earth
opt4: And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities
correct: And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities
explanation: The climax of divine redemption tackles the ultimate root problem: not mere deliverance from geopolitical enemies, but redemption from all sins and guilt. Psalm 130:8 (KJV) - "And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities."

question: By what traditional Latin title is Psalm 130 famously known across church history?
opt1: De Profundis ('Out of the depths')
opt2: Miserere
opt3: Dies Irae
opt4: Stabat Mater
correct: De Profundis ('Out of the depths')
explanation: From the opening words of the Latin Vulgate ('De profundis clamavi ad te, Domine'), Psalm 130 is celebrated worldwide as the 'De Profundis'. Psalm 130:1 (KJV) - "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD."

question: Into which traditional liturgical group of seven psalms does Psalm 130 belong?
opt1: The Messianic Enthronement Psalms
opt2: The Seven Penitential Psalms (Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143)
opt3: The Historical Wisdom Psalms
opt4: The Imprecatory War Psalms
correct: The Seven Penitential Psalms (Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143)
explanation: Psalm 130 is the sixth of the historic Seven Penitential Psalms, central to Christian liturgies of confession, Lent, and repentance. Psalm 130:1-8 (KJV) - "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD ... And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities."

question: Which Protestant Reformer called Psalm 130 a 'Pauline Psalm' because it expounds justification by faith and unmerited forgiveness apart from works?
opt1: John Calvin
opt2: Ulrich Zwingli
opt3: Martin Luther
opt4: John Knox
correct: Martin Luther
explanation: Martin Luther classified Psalm 130 (along with Psalms 32, 51, and 143) as 'Pauline Psalms' because of their clear proclamation of justification by grace alone. Psalm 130:3-4 (KJV) - "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared."

question: What three expressions of ambitious pride does David explicitly renounce in Psalm 131:1?
opt1: A deceitful tongue, slow hands, and seeking counsel from the ungodly
opt2: A proud look, an iron sceptre, and gathering silver from foreign kings
opt3: A haughty heart, lofty eyes, and exercising himself in great matters or things too high for him
opt4: A covetous spirit, boasting in chariots, and building high towers of cedar
correct: A haughty heart, lofty eyes, and exercising himself in great matters or things too high for him
explanation: David repudiates internal pride of heart, external supercilious glances ('lofty eyes'), and intellectual or political presumption ('things too high for me'). Psalm 131:1 (KJV) - "Lord, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me."

question: What tender domestic simile does David use in Psalm 131:2 to describe the peaceful, quiet contentment of his soul?
opt1: As an infant resting upon the breast of his nurse: my spirit is at peace
opt2: As a lamb resting safely in the shepherd's bosom: my heart is calm
opt3: As a dove hidden in the clefts of the rocks: my soul rejoiceth
opt4: As a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child
correct: As a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child
explanation: A newly weaned child has ceased crying, fretting, and demanding milk from its mother; it rests content simply in her loving presence and person. Psalm 131:2 (KJV) - "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child."

question: What concluding national exhortation does David offer in Psalm 131:3 based on his own experience of childlike humility?
opt1: Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever
opt2: Let the tribes of Jacob keep silence before the holy ark
opt3: Let the house of Aaron offer the sacrifices of righteousness
opt4: Let the kings of the earth learn wisdom and serve the LORD with fear
correct: Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever
explanation: David calls the entire covenant commonwealth to renounce restless political intrigue and quiet their souls in perpetual hope in Yahweh. Psalm 131:3 (KJV) - "Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever."

question: What active spiritual discipline of self-control does David describe in Psalm 131:2 before attaining this peace?
opt1: 'I have fasted forty days and nights'
opt2: 'Surely I have behaved and quieted myself'
opt3: 'I have retreated into the wilderness of Judah'
opt4: 'I have laid my hand upon my mouth in silence'
correct: 'Surely I have behaved and quieted myself'
explanation: Contentment is not an automatic passive state; it requires intentional, disciplined composure: actively leveling and calming one's restless soul. Psalm 131:2 (KJV) - "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child."

question: What is the profound theological distinction between an 'unweaned' infant and a 'weaned child' in Psalm 131:2?
opt1: An unweaned infant can speak words of wisdom, while a weaned child is completely silent
opt2: An unweaned infant is unclean under Levitical law, while a weaned child is consecrated
opt3: An unweaned infant clings to the mother merely for what it can extract (milk); a weaned child rests in the mother simply for who she is (fellowship and love)
opt4: An unweaned infant lives in the city, while a weaned child is sent to herd sheep in the hills
correct: An unweaned infant clings to the mother merely for what it can extract (milk); a weaned child rests in the mother simply for who she is (fellowship and love)
explanation: Spiritual maturity means loving God for His glorious self, rather than treating Him merely as a source of immediate emotional or material gratification. Psalm 131:2 (KJV) - "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child."

question: What biblical characters stand in stark negative contrast to David's humble refusal to 'exercise himself in great matters' in Psalm 131:1?
opt1: Jonathan who loved David as his own soul
opt2: Samuel who judged Israel in integrity from his youth
opt3: Barzillai the Gileadite who provided for the king at Mahanaim
opt4: King Saul who grasped at power, and Absalom who conspired proudly to steal the kingdom
correct: King Saul who grasped at power, and Absalom who conspired proudly to steal the kingdom
explanation: While Saul raged with jealous insecurity and Absalom rebelled through vain ambition, David waited patiently on God without grasping at things too high. Psalm 131:1 (KJV) - "Lord, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me."

question: How many verses comprise Psalm 131, ranking it among the shortest and most intimate psalms in the Psalter?
opt1: Exactly three verses
opt2: Exactly five verses
opt3: Exactly seven verses
opt4: Exactly two verses
correct: Exactly three verses
explanation: Psalm 131 is an exquisite poetic miniature of only three verses, matched in brevity only by Psalms 133 and 134 among the Songs of Ascents. Psalm 131:1-3 (KJV) - "Lord, my heart is not haughty ... Surely I have behaved and quieted myself ... Let Israel hope in the LORD from henceforth and for ever."

question: What does David mean by refusing to exercise himself in 'things too high for me'?
opt1: Refusing to climb the highest peaks of Mount Hermon
opt2: Humbly surrendering the incomprehensible secret counsels, sovereign providences, and mysteries of God rather than demanding explanations
opt3: Declining to construct the second story of his royal palace
opt4: Refusing to sing soprano melodies in the temple choir
correct: Humbly surrendering the incomprehensible secret counsels, sovereign providences, and mysteries of God rather than demanding explanations
explanation: True humility acknowledges creaturely limitations, submitting peacefully to the hidden things that belong unto the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29). Psalm 131:1 (KJV) - "Lord, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me."

question: Who is credited with authorship in the heading of Psalm 131?
opt1: Solomon
opt2: Moses
opt3: David ('A Song of degrees of David')
opt4: Hezekiah
correct: David ('A Song of degrees of David')
explanation: The superscription attributes this jewel of quiet contentment directly to King David. Psalm 131:Title (KJV) - "A Song of degrees of David."

question: Which teaching of Jesus Christ in the Gospels perfectly reflects the spiritual truth of Psalm 131?
opt1: 'Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's'
opt2: 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees'
opt3: 'Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature'
opt4: 'Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 18:3)
correct: 'Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 18:3)
explanation: Christ's foundational requirement for kingdom entry—childlike humility, trust, and freedom from self-promotion—is the exact heartbeat of Psalm 131. Psalm 131:2 (KJV) - "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child."

question: What does the psalmist ask the Lord to remember in the opening prayer of Psalm 132:1?
opt1: Lord, remember Abraham, and the covenant of circumcision
opt2: Lord, remember Moses, and the giving of the holy law
opt3: Lord, remember Solomon, and the dedication of the temple
opt4: Lord, remember David, and all his afflictions
correct: Lord, remember David, and all his afflictions
explanation: The psalm appeals to God's covenant loyalty, invoking David's self-sacrificial toils and intense hardships in securing a resting place for the Ark. Psalm 132:1 (KJV) - "Lord, remember David, and all his afflictions:"

question: What solemn vow did David swear to the Mighty God of Jacob in Psalm 132:3-5?
opt1: Surely I will not come into my house, nor go up into my bed, nor give sleep to mine eyes, until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob
opt2: Surely I will not taste wine, nor eat pleasant bread, until the Philistines are conquered and their idols burned
opt3: Surely I will not wear the royal crown, nor sit upon the throne of ivory, until the temple walls are completed
opt4: Surely I will not take a wife, nor build palaces of cedar, until the ark is brought into the Holy of Holies
correct: Surely I will not come into my house, nor go up into my bed, nor give sleep to mine eyes, until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob
explanation: David prioritized God's dwelling above his own domestic comfort, refusing restful sleep until a permanent resting sanctuary was established for Yahweh. Psalm 132:3-5 (KJV) - "Surely I will not come into the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed; I will not give sleep to mine eyes, or slumber to mine eyelids, Until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob."

question: Where does the community recount hearing of and rediscovering the long-neglected Ark of the Covenant in Psalm 132:6?
opt1: Lo, we heard of it at Hebron: we found it in the caves of Adullam
opt2: Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood
opt3: Lo, we heard of it at Shiloh: we found it in the temple of Dagon
opt4: Lo, we heard of it at Bethel: we found it on the threshingfloor of Ornan
correct: Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood
explanation: The Ark was remembered in Bethlehem ('Ephratah') and recovered from the forested settlement of Kirjath-jearim ('the fields of the wood' / Jaar, 1 Samuel 7:1-2). Psalm 132:6 (KJV) - "Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood."

question: What historic procession prayer invites God and the Ark into the newly built temple in Psalm 132:8?
opt1: Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors
opt2: The LORD reigneth; let the people tremble; he sitteth between the cherubims
opt3: Arise, O LORD, into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength
opt4: Stand up, O Lord of hosts, and fill this house with the cloud of thy glory
correct: Arise, O LORD, into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength
explanation: Quoting Moses (Numbers 10:35) and Solomon's dedication prayer (2 Chronicles 6:41), the community welcomes Yahweh and the sacred Ark into their permanent rest. Psalm 132:8 (KJV) - "Arise, O LORD, into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength."

question: With what vestments are the priests prayed to be clothed, and what is the saints' response in Psalm 132:9?
opt1: Let thy priests be clothed with fine linen; and let thy saints weep before the altar
opt2: Let thy priests be clothed with gold and gems; and let thy saints offer bullocks
opt3: Let thy priests be clothed with salvation; and let thy saints blow silver trumpets
opt4: Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints shout for joy
correct: Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints shout for joy
explanation: True ministerial beauty is moral righteousness, and the natural fruit of holy sacerdotal ministry is jubilant praise among God's covenant saints. Psalm 132:9 (KJV) - "Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints shout for joy."

question: What unshakeable covenant oath did the LORD swear unto David in Psalm 132:11?
opt1: The LORD hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne
opt2: I will give thee the riches of Solomon, and thy name shall be great among the heathen
opt3: Thy seed shall build an earthly house of marble that shall endure until the end of the world
opt4: Thou shalt conquer all the kings of the north, and thy borders shall reach the Euphrates
correct: The LORD hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne
explanation: God responds to David's oath with a divine, immutable covenant oath: an unbroken Davidic royal lineage culminating in King Messiah (Acts 2:30). Psalm 132:11 (KJV) - "The LORD hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne."

question: What eternal choice and desire did the Lord declare concerning Zion in Psalm 132:13-14?
opt1: The LORD hath pitched His tent in Jerusalem for seventy years of blessing
opt2: For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it
opt3: The LORD hath selected Mount Moriah to be the place of burnt sacrifices only
opt4: The LORD hath set His throne in the heavens, but Zion is His footstool for a season
correct: For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it
explanation: Zion is not an arbitrary human choice, but Yahweh's sovereign, eternal election—His desired celestial and earthly dwelling place forever. Psalm 132:13-14 (KJV) - "For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it."

question: What compassionate economic and spiritual promise does God make to the needy of Zion in Psalm 132:15?
opt1: I will fill her treasuries with the silver of Tyre and the gold of Ophir
opt2: I will give her vineyards to the Levites, and her corn to the priests
opt3: I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread
opt4: I will release all debts every seventh year, and banish poverty from her streets
correct: I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread
explanation: In God's theocratic kingdom, physical sustenance and welfare for the vulnerable poor are guaranteed by direct divine blessing upon food supplies. Psalm 132:15 (KJV) - "I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread."

question: How does God surpass the prayer of verse 9 ('clothed with righteousness') in His divine answer in Psalm 132:16?
opt1: I will crown her priests with gold diadems: and her saints shall inherit the earth
opt2: I will anoint her priests with holy oil: and her saints shall dance with timbrels
opt3: I will give her priests authority over kings: and her saints shall reign forever
opt4: I will also clothe her priests with salvation: and her saints shall shout aloud for joy
correct: I will also clothe her priests with salvation: and her saints shall shout aloud for joy
explanation: God answers prayer exceedingly abundantly: where they prayed for priests to be clothed with 'righteousness', God clothes them with 'salvation' itself! Psalm 132:16 (KJV) - "I will also clothe her priests with salvation: and her saints shall shout aloud for joy."

question: What two vivid Messianic symbols are ordained for the house of David in the triumphant conclusion of Psalm 132:17-18?
opt1: Making the horn of David to bud, and ordaining a lamp for His anointed, while His crown flourisheth
opt2: Giving the sceptre of Judah to Solomon, and building a throne of twelve lions
opt3: Raising up a branch of cedar in Lebanon, and setting a diadem upon Zerubbabel
opt4: Giving the sword of Goliath to the king, and establishing a fortress of brass
correct: Making the horn of David to bud, and ordaining a lamp for His anointed, while His crown flourisheth
explanation: The 'budding horn' represents surging Messianic power (Luke 1:69), the 'lamp' denotes perpetual Davidic testimony, and the flourishing crown depicts Christ's eternal kingdom. Psalm 132:17-18 (KJV) - "There will I make the horn of David to bud: I have ordained a lamp for mine anointed. His enemies will I clothe with shame: but upon himself shall his crown flourish."

question: What exclamation of praise celebrates fraternal communion in the opening verse of Psalm 133?
opt1: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
opt2: Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants that stand in His house
opt3: Praise the LORD for His goodness, and for His wonderful works to men
opt4: Blessed are they that dwell in thy courts, they will be still praising thee
correct: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
explanation: David celebrates the exquisite beauty of covenant harmony: brotherly unity is both morally 'good' (*tov*) and emotionally 'pleasant' (*na'im*). Psalm 133:1 (KJV) - "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!"

question: To what sacred fragrant oil does Psalm 133:2 compare this brotherly unity?
opt1: The pure olive oil burned in the golden lamps of the holy place
opt2: The precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments
opt3: The royal oil of anointing poured upon the horn of David at Bethlehem

opt4: Play upon your instruments to the glory of the god Bel
correct: Sing us one of the songs of Zion
explanation: The captors maliciously demanded entertainment and sport, demanding that the weeping captives chant their sacred temple songs of Zion for amusement. Psalm 137:3 (KJV) - "For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion."

question: What principled refusal do the faithful captives voice in Psalm 137:4?
opt1: Shall we cast holy pearls before swine and dogs?
opt2: Can a captive rejoice while the holy city lieth desolate in ashes?
opt3: Will God accept praise from the polluted soil of the heathen?
opt4: How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?
correct: How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?
explanation: Temple songs were sacred acts of worship to Yahweh; singing them as foreign cabaret entertainment in an unclean, pagan land was unthinkable sacrilege. Psalm 137:4 (KJV) - "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?"

question: What self-imprecation does the musician invoke upon his musical skill if he ever forgets Jerusalem in Psalm 137:5?
opt1: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning
opt2: If I forget thee, O Zion, let mine eyes be blinded with darkness
opt3: If I cease to remember thee, let my fingers be broken like reed
opt4: If I love Babylon, let my harp strings be snapped in twain
correct: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning
explanation: The harpist invokes immediate paralysis on his strumming right hand: if he ever forgets Jerusalem, let his hand lose all its musical skill ('cunning'). Psalm 137:5 (KJV) - "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning."

question: What physical penalty does the singer pronounce upon his vocal organs in Psalm 137:6?
opt1: Let my voice be turned to mourning, and my throat be dried like a potsherd
opt2: Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy
opt3: Let my lips be struck dumb, that I may never utter a psalm of praise
opt4: Let my mouth be filled with dust, if I delight in the palaces of Babel
correct: Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy
explanation: If Jerusalem is not cherished as supreme over every earthly happiness ('above my chief joy'), the singer vows never to speak or sing again. Psalm 137:6 (KJV) - "If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy."

question: What treacherous, bloodthirsty cry of the Edomites during Jerusalem's fall is remembered in Psalm 137:7?
opt1: Slay the priests and burn the temple with fire
opt2: Divide the spoils of Judah and let none escape to the mountains
opt3: Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof
opt4: Let Babylon conquer Salem and give us her vineyards
correct: Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof
explanation: When Babylon besieged Jerusalem, brother Esau's descendants (Edom) cheered on the demolition, screaming: 'Rase it! (Tear it down to the bedrock!)' (Obadiah 1:10-14). Psalm 137:7 (KJV) - "Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof."

question: What prophetic retribution is pronounced upon Babylon in Psalm 137:8?
opt1: O city of idols, who art fallen; joyful shall be the exiles who return to Zion
opt2: O throne of pride, who art cast into the pit; blessed be the king of Persia who breaketh thy gates
opt3: O land of Chaldea, whose rivers shall dry up; holy is the Lord who consumeth thee with fire
opt4: O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us
correct: O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us
explanation: Under the divine law of retribution (lex talionis), Babylon is doomed to receive exactly the merciless atrocities she inflicted upon conquered nations. Psalm 137:8 (KJV) - "O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us."

question: What harrowing ancient Near Eastern warfare atrocity (prophesied in Isaiah 13:16) is mentioned in Psalm 137:9 as returning upon Babylon?
opt1: Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones
opt2: He that burneth thy high towers and soweth thy palaces with salt
opt3: He that leadeth thy nobles in iron chains into the mountains of Media
opt4: He that casteth thy idols into the river and hangeth thy king on a tree
correct: Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones
explanation: Reflecting the raw, horrific realities of ancient conquest, the psalm echoes Isaiah 13:16, declaring that Babylon's own brutal slaughter of infants would rebound upon her. Psalm 137:9 (KJV) - "Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones."

question: Which specific Babylonian rivers provided the setting for the weeping exiles in verse 1?
opt1: The Nile and the river of Goshen
opt2: The Euphrates and its vast irrigation canal network, including the River Chebar where Ezekiel saw visions (Ezekiel 1:1)
opt3: The Jordan and the brook Kidron
opt4: The Orontes and the river of Damascus
correct: The Euphrates and its vast irrigation canal network, including the River Chebar where Ezekiel saw visions (Ezekiel 1:1)
explanation: Babylon was crisscrossed by major waterways—the Euphrates, Tigris, and extensive canals like the Chebar—beside which Jewish exiles gathered to lament. Psalm 137:1 (KJV) - "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."

question: With what intensity and before whom does David declare he will sing praise in Psalm 138:1?
opt1: I will praise thee with loud cymbals: before the congregation of Judah will I sing
opt2: I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee
opt3: I will praise thee with early morning prayers: before the high priest will I bow
opt4: I will praise thee with a solemn vow: before the armies of Israel will I rejoice
correct: I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee
explanation: David offers undivided devotion ('with my whole heart') in the presence of celestial angels and earthly judges/rulers ('before the gods' / *elohim*). Psalm 138:1 (KJV) - "I will praise thee with my whole heart: before the gods will I sing praise unto thee."

question: What astonishing declaration regarding the supreme honor God has placed upon His written revelation appears in Psalm 138:2?
opt1: For thou hast established thy throne above all the heavens
opt2: For thou hast made thy covenant stronger than the pillars of the earth
opt3: For thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name
opt4: For thou hast revealed thy salvation in the sight of the heathen
correct: For thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name
explanation: God has elevated the veracity, authority, and fidelity of His promises ('thy word') to the highest pinnacle of divine majesty ('above all thy name'). Psalm 138:2 (KJV) - "I will worship toward thy holy temple, and praise thy name for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name."

question: What immediate internal transformation occurred when David cried out to God in Psalm 138:3?
opt1: In the night when I prayed an angel delivered me from the hand of Saul
opt2: When I called from the pit thou broughtest my feet upon a high mountain
opt3: When I wept before the ark thou gavest me victory over the Philistines
opt4: In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul
correct: In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul
explanation: God did not merely change outward circumstances; He infused supernatural courage and spiritual endurance directly into David's inner man ('strength in my soul'). Psalm 138:3 (KJV) - "In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul."

question: What global response will earthly monarchs display when they hear the words of the Lord's mouth in Psalm 138:4-5?
opt1: All the kings of the earth shall praise thee, O LORD ... Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the LORD: for great is the glory of the LORD
opt2: All the kings shall cast their crowns into the dust and tremble at His holiness
opt3: All the princes shall bring tribute of gold and silver into the temple of Zion
opt4: All emperors shall confess that their kingdoms are vanity before the God of Jacob
correct: All the kings of the earth shall praise thee, O LORD ... Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the LORD: for great is the glory of the LORD
explanation: Earthly monarchs will be captivated by the majesty of God's Word, becoming joyful worshippers singing in the righteous ways of Yahweh. Psalm 138:4-5 (KJV) - "All the kings of the earth shall praise thee, O LORD, when they hear the words of thy mouth. Yea, they shall sing in the ways of the LORD: for great is the glory of the LORD."

question: What profound paradox regarding God's posture toward the lowly versus the proud is proclaimed in Psalm 138:6?
opt1: Though the Lord ruleth over all, He blesseth the rich: but the simple He passeth by
opt2: Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off
opt3: The Lord sitteth in the heavens, judging the righteous: but the wicked He destroyeth with fire
opt4: The Lord is a consuming fire to the rebellious: but a gentle shepherd to the strong
correct: Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off
explanation: God draws intimately near to the humble and contrite, but maintains cold, aloof distance from the self-sufficient and arrogant ('knoweth afar off'). Psalm 138:6 (KJV) - "Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off."

question: What confidence of revival and divine rescue does David express when surrounded by crisis in Psalm 138:7?
opt1: Though an host encamp against me, my heart shall not fear: for angels shall build a wall around my camp
opt2: Though I pass through the shadow of death, no evil shall touch me: for thy rod and staff comfort me
opt3: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me
opt4: Though the waters roar and the mountains shake, I shall abide: for God is my refuge and strength
correct: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me
explanation: Even when completely enveloped by crisis, God revitalizes the believer's spirit and deploys His victorious right hand to neutralize enemy wrath. Psalm 138:7 (KJV) - "Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me."

question: What triumphant assurance of divine completion and lifelong mercy concludes Psalm 138:8?
opt1: The Lord will establish the throne of David forever: His kingdom shall have no end: praise ye the Lord
opt2: The Lord will satisfy my soul with good things: my horn shall be exalted: Selah
opt3: The Lord will keep my going out and my coming in: He will preserve my soul from all evil
opt4: The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands
correct: The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands
explanation: God will faithfully finish and bring to mature perfection every detail of His purposeful plan for the believer, never abandoning His personal workmanship. Psalm 138:8 (KJV) - "The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands."

question: Which New Testament promise in Philippians 1:6 directly mirrors the assurance of Psalm 138:8 ('The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me')?
opt1: 'He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ'
opt2: 'All things work together for good to them that love God'
opt3: 'I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me'
opt4: 'My God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory'
correct: 'He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ'
explanation: Paul's conviction in Philippians 1:6 that God completes the good work He started is the exact New Testament exposition of Psalm 138:8. Psalm 138:8 (KJV) - "The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands."

question: What unique canonical position does Psalm 138 occupy in the Book of Psalms?
opt1: It is the concluding doxology of Book IV of the Psalms
opt2: It opens the final collection of eight Davidic psalms (Psalms 138-145) concluding King David's contributions to the Psalter
opt3: It is the central psalm among the Songs of Ascents
opt4: It is the opening psalm of the final Five Hallelujah Psalms
correct: It opens the final collection of eight Davidic psalms (Psalms 138-145) concluding King David's contributions to the Psalter
explanation: Following the Songs of Ascents (120-134) and temple praise (135-137), Psalm 138 inaugurates the final octet of David's inspired compositions (138-145). Psalm 138:Title (KJV) - "A Psalm of David."

question: Toward what architectural sanctuary did David worship when offering this thanksgiving in Psalm 138:2?
opt1: Toward the ark in the tent of Zion
opt2: Toward the high place of Gibeon
opt3: Toward thy holy temple
opt4: Toward Mount Sinai in Arabia
correct: Toward thy holy temple
explanation: David directed his prayers toward God's consecrated earthly sanctuary ('holy temple' / *heikhal*), whether the tabernacle in Zion or the heavenly archetype. Psalm 138:2 (KJV) - "I will worship toward thy holy temple, and praise thy name for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name."

question: What comprehensive divine omniscience does David celebrate in Psalm 139:2-4?
opt1: God numbers the hairs of his head, counts the sands of the sea, and knows the names of the stars
opt2: God records all his tears in a bottle, weighs his actions in a balance, and sets an angel over his steps
opt3: God knows his downsitting and uprising, understands his thoughts afar off, compasses his path, and knows every word before it is spoken
opt4: God perceives the secrets of the kings of the earth, knows the foundations of the world, and judges the nations
correct: God knows his downsitting and uprising, understands his thoughts afar off, compasses his path, and knows every word before it is spoken
explanation: God possesses total, exhaustive foreknowledge of all physical movements, unspoken inner thoughts, daily paths, and future speech. Psalm 139:2-4 (KJV) - "Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether."

question: How does David describe the inescapable omnipresence of God's Spirit in Psalm 139:8?
opt1: If I fly to the ends of the earth, thy glory is seen: if I hide in the caves, thy voice is heard
opt2: If I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, thy rod is near: if I dwell in the palace, thy peace is with me
opt3: If I plunge into the depths of the ocean, thy light shineth: if I stand upon Mount Hermon, thy presence encompasseth me
opt4: If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there
correct: If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there
explanation: No spatial boundary in the cosmos can escape God's presence: neither the highest celestial heights ('heaven') nor the deepest subterranean depths of the grave ('hell' / Sheol). Psalm 139:8 (KJV) - "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there."

question: What geographic flight on the 'wings of the morning' is described in Psalm 139:9-10, and what meets the traveler there?
opt1: Dwelling in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me
opt2: Fleeing to the western borders of the Mediterranean; even there shall the tempest overtake me
opt3: Ascending to the golden gates of the sunrise; even there shall thy holy angels surround me
opt4: Hiding in the desert islands of the Gentiles; even there shall thy righteous judgment find me
correct: Dwelling in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me
explanation: Even if one could speed westward with the velocity of morning sunlight to the most distant maritime frontier, God's guiding and holding hand is already there. Psalm 139:9-10 (KJV) - "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me."

question: How does physical darkness appear from the perspective of God's all-seeing eye in Psalm 139:12?
opt1: The darkness is as a veil of smoke, but thy glory pierceth it as an arrow of fire
opt2: The darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee
opt3: The night is as thick clouds before the throne, but thine eyes see through the depths
opt4: The shadow of death covereth all flesh, but the Lord of hosts dwelleth in uncreated light
correct: The darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee
explanation: Darkness presents zero obstruction to divine vision; to the omniscient Creator, pitch-black night is as transparent and luminous as blazing noonday. Psalm 139:12 (KJV) - "Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee."

question: What famous praise does the psalmist utter concerning his embryonic development in Psalm 139:14?
opt1: I will give thanks; for thou hast crowned me with glory and honor: thou hast put all things under my feet
opt2: I will bless the Lord; for thou hast formed my spirit within me: thou hast breathed the breath of life
opt3: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well
opt4: I will rejoice; for thou hast chosen me from my mother's womb: thou hast set my name in the book of life
correct: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well
explanation: The intricate biological engineering of the human body evokes holy awe ('fearfully and wonderfully made') toward the divine Craftsman. Psalm 139:14 (KJV) - "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well."

question: What prenatal blueprint recorded in God's book is described in Psalm 139:16?
opt1: Thine angels did mold my flesh out of clay; and in the archives of heaven my years were numbered
opt2: Thy wisdom did weigh my bones in the secret place; and all the days of my life were ordained before the sun
opt3: Thou didst know my spirit before the world was founded; and my name was sealed for the kingdom
opt4: Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them
correct: Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them
explanation: Before microscopic embryonic tissue ('substance, yet being unperfect') developed into distinct limbs and organs, God's architectural book had mapped out every detail. Psalm 139:16 (KJV) - "Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them."

question: How does David evaluate the number and preciousness of God's thoughts toward him in Psalm 139:17-18?
opt1: How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them! If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand
opt2: Thy thoughts are deep like the ocean; they surpass the wisdom of the angels of light
opt3: Thy counsels are righteous from everlasting; they are more glorious than the stars of heaven
opt4: Thy thoughts are pure as refined silver; the sum of them is sweeter than honey to my taste
correct: How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them! If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand
explanation: God's attentive, loving thoughts toward the believer are infinitely vast and innumerable, exceeding the grains of sand on all the world's seashores. Psalm 139:17-18 (KJV) - "How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! how great is the sum of them! If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee."

question: How does David describe his moral separation from defiant blasphemers in Psalm 139:21-22?
opt1: I pray that their eyes may be enlightened, that they may turn from their idols to the living God
opt2: Do not I hate them, O LORD, that hate thee? and am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee? I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies
opt3: I have separated myself from their tents, and have not eaten of their sacrifices in the groves
opt4: I have delivered them unto the sword of justice, and their memory shall perish from the earth
correct: Do not I hate them, O LORD, that hate thee? and am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee? I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies
explanation: 'Perfect hatred' is not petty personal malice, but total, uncompromised loyalty to God that views God's enemies as one's own adversaries. Psalm 139:21-22 (KJV) - "Do not I hate them, O LORD, that hate thee? and am not I grieved with those that rise up against thee? I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies."

question: With what humble, searching petition of total spiritual surrender does Psalm 139 conclude in verses 23-24?
opt1: Deliver me from all mine iniquities: wash me thoroughly from my sin, and restore the joy of salvation
opt2: Create in me a clean heart, O God: renew a right spirit within me, and take not thy holy spirit from me
opt3: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting
opt4: Preserve my soul from the snare of the fowler: keep my feet from falling, and bring me to Zion
correct: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting
explanation: Aware of deceitful self-blindness, David invites the omniscient God to perform an exhaustive heart audit, purging any latent sin and guiding him into eternal paths. Psalm 139:23-24 (KJV) - "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting."

question: Into what four symmetrical six-verse theological movements is Psalm 139 structured?
opt1: 1) Morning prayer, 2) Noon battle, 3) Evening reflection, 4) Midnight watch
opt2: 1) Praise of Israel, 2) Fall of Egypt, 3) Wilderness journey, 4) Conquest of Canaan
opt3: 1) Confession of sin, 2) Pardon of guilt, 3) Animal sacrifice, 4) Priestly blessing
opt4: 1) Omniscience (vv. 1-6), 2) Omnipresence (vv. 7-12), 3) Omnipotence/Creation (vv. 13-18), 4) Moral Consecration (vv. 19-24)
correct: 1) Omniscience (vv. 1-6), 2) Omnipresence (vv. 7-12), 3) Omnipotence/Creation (vv. 13-18), 4) Moral Consecration (vv. 19-24)
explanation: Psalm 139 unfolds with architectural perfection: four strophes of six verses each exploring God's all-knowing mind, all-present Spirit, all-powerful hands, and holy character. Psalm 139:1, 7, 13, 23 (KJV) - "thou hast searched me, and known me ... Whither shall I go from thy spirit ... For thou hast possessed my reins ... Search me, O God, and know my heart:"

question: From what two characterizations of wicked persecutors does David plead for deliverance in Psalm 140:1?
opt1: The proud prince and the deceitful counselor
opt2: The strange woman and the hypocritical priest
opt3: The foreign invader and the covetous neighbor
opt4: The evil man and the violent man
correct: The evil man and the violent man
explanation: David petitions Yahweh to rescue him from corrupt malice ('the evil man') and lawless physical brutality ('the violent man'). Psalm 140:1 (KJV) - "Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man: preserve me from the violent man;"

question: What venomous anatomical metaphor in Psalm 140:3 describes the speech of slanderers, quoted by Paul in Romans 3:13?
opt1: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips
opt2: Their throat is an open sepulchre; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness
opt3: Their tongue is a sharp razor, working deceitfully and devouring the innocent
opt4: Their words are drawn swords; the venom of asps is in their belly
correct: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips
explanation: The Apostle Paul cites Psalm 140:3 in his indictment of human depravity: slanderous lips conceal lethal viper venom. Psalm 140:3 (KJV) - "They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; adders' poison is under their lips. Selah."

question: Which four concealed hunting devices of the proud are enumerated in Psalm 140:5?
opt1: Pits of clay, sharpened stakes, concealed arrows, and iron chains
opt2: A snare, cords, a net by the wayside, and gins
opt3: False witnesses, secret bribes, lying warrants, and hidden daggers
opt4: Poisoned meat, deep trenches, fiery darts, and stumbling blocks
correct: A snare, cords, a net by the wayside, and gins
explanation: Depicting insidious spiritual and political ambushes, the text lists fowling snares, trip-cords, roadside drag-nets, and baited spring-traps ('gins'). Psalm 140:5 (KJV) - "The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah."

question: What military protection did God provide for David in the midst of conflict according to Psalm 140:7?
opt1: Thou hast girded my loins with a belt of strength
opt2: Thou hast shod my feet with the preparation of peace
opt3: Thou hast covered my head in the day of battle
opt4: Thou hast given mine enemies into the palm of my hand
correct: Thou hast covered my head in the day of battle
explanation: God acted as an impenetrable bronze war-helmet, deflecting deadly blows and preserving David's life in the heat of combat. Psalm 140:7 (KJV) - "O GOD the Lord, the strength of my salvation, thou hast covered my head in the day of battle."

question: What poetic justice does David pray will rebound upon his slanderous conspirators in Psalm 140:9?
opt1: Let their swords enter into their own bowels
opt2: Let their houses be consumed with their own torches
opt3: Let their children be taken in their own traps
opt4: Let the mischief of their own lips cover them
correct: Let the mischief of their own lips cover them
explanation: The very malicious lies and destructive slander hatched by the conspirators' lips are prayed to crash back over their own heads. Psalm 140:9 (KJV) - "As for the head of those that compass me about, let the mischief of their own lips cover them."

question: What terrifying imagery of divine retributive judgment appears in Psalm 140:10?
opt1: Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again
opt2: Let the whirlwind scatter their bones: let the beasts of the desert devour their carcasses
opt3: Let the heavens drop brimstone upon their tents: let them be drowned in the Red sea
opt4: Let their eyes fail with weeping: let their memory be blotted out from under heaven
correct: Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again
explanation: Echoing the historic catastrophe of Sodom, David invokes falling coals of fire and bottomless pits to swallow unrepentant violent persecutors. Psalm 140:10 (KJV) - "Let burning coals fall upon them: let them be cast into the fire; into deep pits, that they rise not up again."

question: How does Psalm 140:11 portray the inevitable self-destruction of the violent man?
opt1: The sword of justice shall overtake him in the gate
opt2: Evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him
opt3: The arrows of the Almighty shall pierce him in his bedchamber
opt4: The angel of the Lord shall pursue him into outer darkness
correct: Evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him
explanation: Sin is its own relentless bloodhound: the very wickedness a violent man breeds tracks him down like a beast of prey to destroy him. Psalm 140:11 (KJV) - "Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him."

question: What certainty does the psalmist possess regarding the judicial defense of the oppressed in Psalm 140:12?
opt1: I know that the king will avenge the blood of the righteous upon the mountains
opt2: I know that the judges of Israel will take no bribe from the violent man
opt3: I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor
opt4: I know that the temple priests will offer atonement for the destitute
correct: I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor
explanation: Though earthly courts fail, the supreme cosmic Court of Heaven unfailingly champions the cause and rights of the powerless poor. Psalm 140:12 (KJV) - "I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor."

question: Where are the upright promised to dwell in the serene conclusion of Psalm 140:13?
opt1: In the palaces of Jerusalem
opt2: In the green pastures of peace
opt3: Upon the holy mountain of David
